questions.q: In the figure, the values of currents I$_1$, I$_2$ and I$_3$ respectively are [Figure: 5A enters a junction from the left and 1A leaves the same junction downward-then-left; the remaining current I$_1$ continues right to a second junction where 1.5A leaves to the right and I$_2$ continues down; I$_2$ reaches a third junction where another 1.5A leaves to the right and I$_3$ continues down]
questions.explanation: At the first junction: 5A = I$_1$ + 1A ⟹ I$_1$ = 4A. At the second junction: I$_1$ = 1.5A + I$_2$ ⟹ I$_2$ = 2.5A. At the third junction: I$_2$ = 1.5A + I$_3$ ⟹ I$_3$ = 1A.

questions.q: The number of electrons moving per second through the filament of a lamp of 60W operating at 120V is nearly (e = 1.6 × 10$^{-19}$ C) ______

Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The resistivity of a conductor is independent of its temperature
Statement II: The resistivity of a semiconductor decreases with increase in temperature
Select the correct option.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation: A conductor's resistivity increases with temperature (Statement I is false); a semiconductor's resistivity decreases with temperature as more charge carriers are thermally freed (Statement II is true).

questions.q: Current flowing through a wire decreases linearly from 10A to zero in 4s as shown in the graph. Find the total charge flowing through the wire in the given time interval. [Figure: I-t graph, a straight line decreasing linearly from I = 10A at t = 0 to I = 0 at t = 4s]
questions.explanation: Charge = area under the I-t graph = ½ × base × height = ½ × 4 × 10 = 20C.

questions.q: In a conducting region, 10$^{19}$ electrons and 10$^{19}$ protons move to the left, while 10$^{19}$ α-particles move to the right per second. The resulting electric current is (e = 1.6 × 10$^{-19}$ C) ______
questions.explanation: Electrons moving left give a conventional current of 1.6A to the right; protons moving left give 1.6A to the left; α-particles (charge 2e) moving right give 3.2A to the right. Net current = (1.6+3.2) right − 1.6 left = 3.2A towards the right.

questions.q: Which of the following circuits is correct for verification of Ohm's law? [Figure: four circuit diagrams, each with a battery, rheostat, a fixed resistor, an ammeter and a voltmeter connected in different arrangements/polarities]
questions.explanation: The correct circuit places the voltmeter directly across the resistor alone with the ammeter in series with it, and both meters connected with polarity matching the direction of conventional current from the battery, as shown in Figure (2).

questions.q: In the following circuit, the terminal voltage across the cell is [circuit: 2 V cell with internal resistance 0.1 Ω in series with an external resistor of 3.9 Ω]

Two cells of emfs E$_1$ and E$_2$ and internal resistances r$_1$ and r$_2$ (E$_2$ > E$_1$ and r$_2$ > r$_1$) respectively, are connected in parallel as shown in figure. The equivalent emf of the combination is E$_{eq}$. Then
questions.explanation: $E_{eq}=\dfrac{E_1/r_1+E_2/r_2}{1/r_1+1/r_2}$. Since $r_1<r_2$, the branch with $E_1$ is weighted more heavily, pulling $E_{eq}$ closer to $E_1$.

questions.q: The variations of resistivity ρ with absolute temperature T for three different materials X, Y and Z are shown in the graph below. Identify the materials X, Y and Z. [graph: ρ vs T; Z decreases sharply with T, X and Y increase with T, X lying above Y]
options: X – copper, Y – nichrome, Z – semiconductor
X – copper, Y – semiconductor, Z – nichrome
X – semiconductor, Y – nichrome, Z – copper
X – nichrome, Y – copper, Z – semiconductor
questions.explanation: Metals (copper, nichrome) show resistivity increasing with temperature while a semiconductor's resistivity falls sharply as T increases, identifying Z as the semiconductor and X, Y as the two metals as per the KEA key.

questions.q: Given, a current carrying wire of non-uniform cross-section, which of the following is constant throughout the length of wire?
options: Current, electric field and drift speed
questions.explanation: By charge conservation the current I is the same everywhere along the wire; since the area varies, the electric field and drift speed (which depend on area) are not constant.

questions.q: The graph between variation of resistance of a metal wire as a function of its diameter keeping other parameters like length and temperature constant is
options: curve decreasing steeply then levelling off (graph 4)
questions.explanation: $R=\dfrac{\rho L}{A}=\dfrac{4\rho L}{\pi D^2}\propto \dfrac{1}{D^2}$, which is a steadily decreasing curve as shown in graph 4.

questions.q: In an experiment to determine the figure of merit of a galvanometer by half deflection method, a student constructed the following circuit. He unplugged a resistance of 5200 Ω in R. When K$_1$ is closed and K$_2$ is open, the deflection observed in the galvanometer is 26 div. When K$_2$ is also closed and a resistance of 90 Ω is removed in S, the deflection becomes 13 div. The resistance of galvanometer is nearly
questions.explanation: Using the half-deflection method formula $G=\dfrac{RS}{R-S}$ with the resistance box values obtained from the given readings gives $G\approx91.6\,\Omega$ (as per KEA key).

questions.q: $\vec E$ is the electric field inside a conductor whose material has conductivity $\sigma$ and resistivity $\rho$. The current density inside the conductor is $\vec j$. The correct form of Ohm's law is
questions.explanation: From $V=iR$, $\dfrac{V}{\ell}=\dfrac{i}{A}\rho$, which gives $\vec E=\rho\vec j$.

questions.q: In the circuit shown, the end A is at potential $V_0$ and end B is grounded. The electric current I indicated in the circuit is [a repeating ladder network of resistors: series R, then rungs of R, then 2R sections with rungs of 2R, ending at grounded B]
questions.explanation: The repeating ladder network reduces to an effective resistance $R_{eff}=R+2R=3R$, so $I=\dfrac{V_0}{3R}$.

questions.q: The electric current flowing through a given conductor varies with time as shown in the graph below [current I rises linearly from about 100 mA at t=0 to 400 mA at t=10s, then stays constant at 400 mA up to t=20s]. The number of free electrons which flow through a given cross-section of the conductor in the time interval $0\le t\le20s$ is
questions.explanation: The charge $Q=ne$ equals the area under the I-t graph, which works out to $5\,C$; so $n=\dfrac{5}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=3.125\times10^{19}$.

questions.q: The I-V graph for a conductor at two different temperatures $100^0C$ and $400^0C$ is as shown in the figure [two straight lines through the origin, making angles $45^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ with the V-axis]. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the conductor is about (in per degree Celsius)
questions.explanation: $R_1=\cot45^\circ=1$, $R_2=\cot30^\circ=\sqrt3$; $\alpha=\dfrac{R_2-R_1}{R_1t_2-R_2t_1}\approx3\times10^{-3}\,/^\circ C$.

questions.q: An electric blub of 60 W, 120 V is to be connected to 220 V source. What resistance should be connected in series with the bulb, so that the bulb glows properly?
questions.explanation: Bulb resistance $R=\dfrac{V^2}{P}=240\Omega$, rated current $I=0.5A$; required total resistance $=\dfrac{220}{0.5}=440\Omega$, so the series resistance $=440-240=200\Omega$.

questions.q: For a given electric current the drift velocity of conduction electrons in a copper wire is v$_d$ and their mobility is μ. When the current is increased at constant temperature
options: v$_d$ remains the same, μ increases
v$_d$ decreases, μ remains the same
v$_d$ remains the same, μ decreases
v$_d$ increases, μ remains the same
questions.explanation: I = nAev$_d$, so increasing current increases v$_d$ proportionally; mobility μ = v$_d$/E depends on the relaxation time (hence temperature) and stays unchanged at constant temperature.

questions.q: Ten identical cells each emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 Ω are connected in series with two cells wrongly connected. A resistor of 10 Ω is connected to the combination. What is the current through the resistor?
questions.explanation: Net emf = (10−2×2)×2 = 12 V, total internal resistance = 10×1 = 10 Ω. Current = 12/(10+10) = 0.6 A.

questions.q: The equivalent resistance between the points A and B in the following circuit is [a ladder network: A connects through three 2Ω resistors in series along the top (open at the far end), B connects through three 2Ω resistors in series along the bottom (open at the far end), with three 2Ω resistors as vertical rungs joining the top and bottom rails at each junction]
questions.explanation: Reducing from the open (right) end: the rightmost rung (2Ω) in series with the top and bottom 2Ω segments (2+2Ω) forms a 6Ω path in parallel with the middle rung's 2Ω, giving 1.5Ω; that combines with the next 2Ω top+bottom segments (2+2Ω) to form a 5.5Ω path in parallel with the left rung's 2Ω, giving 22/15Ω; adding the outer 2Ω top and bottom segments gives 2+22/15+2 = 82/15 ≈ 5.5 Ω between A and B.

questions.q: The resistance of a carbon resistor is 4.7 kΩ ± 5%. The colour of the third band is
questions.explanation: 4.7 kΩ = 47×10$^2$ Ω: yellow(4)-violet(7)-red(×10$^2$, third band)-gold(±5%).

questions.q: The four bands of a colour coded resistor are of the colours gray, red, gold and gold. The value of the resistance of the resistor is
questions.explanation: gray=8, red=2, gold (third band, multiplier) = ×0.1, gold (fourth band) = ±5% tolerance, giving 82×0.1 = 8.2Ω ± 5%.

questions.q: A wire of resistance R is connected across a cell of emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance r. The current through the circuit is I. In time t, the work done by the battery to establish the current I is
questions.explanation: Work done by the emf source in time t is W = $\varepsilon$It, part of which is dissipated in R and part in the internal resistance r.

questions.q: Ten identical cells each of potential 'E' and internal resistance 'r', are connected in series to form a closed circuit. An ideal voltmeter connected across three cells, will read
questions.note: With no external resistor the loop current is I = 10E/10r = E/r, so the voltmeter across any 3 series cells should read 3E - I(3r) = 3E - 3E = 0, which isn't an option; KEA's key credits 3E (the naive sum of EMFs, ignoring that the same current also flows through those cells' own internal resistance).
questions.explanation: KEA's key credits the simple sum of the three cells' EMFs, 3E, though a full loop analysis (see note) gives 0.

questions.q: In an atom electrons revolve around the nucleus along a path of radius 0.72 Å making 9.4 $\times$ 10$^{18}$ revolutions per second. The equivalent current is $-$ [given e = 1.6 $\times$ 10$^{-19}$ C]
questions.explanation: Equivalent current $I=ef=1.6\times10^{-19}\times9.4\times10^{18}\approx1.5$ A.

questions.q: When a metal conductor connected to left gap of a meter bridge is heated, the balancing point
questions.explanation: Heating a metal increases its resistance; to restore balance ($R_{left}/R_{right}=l/(100-l)$) with a larger left resistance, the balance length l must increase, i.e. the balance point shifts towards the right.

questions.q: A charged particle is moving in an electric field of 3 $\times$ 10$^{-10}$ V m$^{-1}$ with mobility 2.5 $\times$ 10$^6$ m$^2$/Vs, its drift velocity is
questions.explanation: Drift velocity $v_d=\mu E=2.5\times10^6\times3\times10^{-10}=7.5\times10^{-4}$ m/s.

questions.q: Wire bound resistors are made by
options: winding the wires of an alloy of Ge, Au, Ga
winding the wires of an alloy of Cu, Al, Ag
winding the wires of an alloy of manganin, constantan, nichrome
winding the wires of an alloy of Si, Tu, Fe
questions.explanation: Wire-wound resistors are made from high-resistivity, low temperature-coefficient alloys such as manganin, constantan and nichrome.

questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance 50 $\Omega$ is connected to a battery of 3 V along with a resistance of 2950 $\Omega$ in series. A full scale deflection of 30 divisions is obtained in the galvanometer. In order to reduce this deflection to 20 divisions, the resistance in series should be
questions.explanation: Current for 30 divisions: $I_1=3/(50+2950)=1$ mA. For 20 divisions, $I_2=\tfrac{2}{3}\times1\text{ mA}=0.667$ mA $=3/(50+R)$, giving $R=4500-50=4450\ \Omega$.

questions.q: If voltage across a bulb rated 220 V, 100 W drops by 2.5% of its rated value, the percentage of the rated value by which the power would decrease is
questions.explanation: Since $P\propto V^2$, $\dfrac{dP}{P}=2\dfrac{dV}{V}=2\times2.5\%=5\%$.

questions.q: A wire of a certain material is stretched slowly by 10%. Its new resistance and specific resistance becomes respectively
questions.explanation: Volume stays constant, so $A'=A/1.1$ when $L'=1.1L$; $R=\rho L/A$ gives $R'=1.21R$, while resistivity $\rho$ (a material property) stays the same.

questions.q: A wire of resistance 3 Ω is stretched to twice its original length. The resistance of the new wire will be
questions.explanation: For constant volume, $R\propto l^2$, so stretching to twice the length gives $R'=3\times2^2=12\ \Omega$.

questions.q: In the given arrangement of experiment on metre bridge, if AD corresponding to null deflection of the galvanometer is X, what would be its value if the radius of the wire AB is doubled? (Figure: metre bridge circuit with resistances R$_1$, R$_2$ and galvanometer G connected between points A, D, B on wire AB.)
questions.explanation: The balance condition $\dfrac{R_1}{R_2}=\dfrac{\text{resistance of }AD}{\text{resistance of }DB}$ depends only on the length ratio (resistivity and area being uniform along the wire), so it is independent of the wire's radius; the null point X remains unchanged.

questions.q: A copper wire of length 1 m and uniform crosssectional area 5 $\times$ 10$^{-7}$ m$^2$ carries a current of 1A. Assuming that there are 8 $\times$ 10$^{28}$ free electrons per m$^3$ in copper, how long will an electron take to drift from one end of the wire to the other?
questions.explanation: $v_d=\dfrac{I}{nAe}=\dfrac{1}{(8\times10^{28})(5\times10^{-7})(1.6\times10^{-19})}\approx1.56\times10^{-4}$ m/s; time $=\dfrac{l}{v_d}=\dfrac{1}{1.56\times10^{-4}}\approx6.4\times10^3$ s.

questions.q: Consider an electrical conductor connected across a potential difference V. Let $\Delta q$ be a small charge moving through it in time $\Delta t$. If I is the electric current through it, (I) the kinetic energy of the charge increases by IV$\Delta t$. (II) the electric potential energy of the charge decreases by IV$\Delta t$. (III) the thermal energy of the conductor increases by IV$\Delta t$. Then the correct statement/s is / are
questions.explanation: The drift speed (and hence average KE of charge carriers) stays essentially constant; the electric PE lost by the charge as it moves through the potential difference (IV$\Delta t$) is entirely converted into thermal (Joule heating) energy of the conductor, so (II) and (III) are correct.

questions.q: A metal rod of length 10 cm and a rectangular cross-section of 1 cm $\times \dfrac{1}{2}$ cm is connected to a battery across opposite faces. The resistance will be
options: same irrespective of the three faces.
maximum when the battery is connected across 1 cm $\times \dfrac12$ cm faces.
maximum when the battery is connected across 10 cm $\times \dfrac12$ cm faces.
maximum when the battery is connected across 10 cm $\times$ 1 cm faces.
questions.explanation: $R=\rho L/A$ is largest when the current path (length) is the longest and the cross-section is smallest, i.e. when connected across the $1\times\tfrac12$ cm faces, making the 10 cm dimension the length.

questions.q: A car has a fresh storage battery of e.m.f. 12 V and internal resistance $2\times10^{-2}\,\Omega$. If the starter motor draws a current of 80 A, then the terminal voltage when the starter is on is
The colour code for a carbon resistor of resistance $0.28\,\text{k}\Omega \pm 10\%$ is
questions.explanation: $280\,\Omega=28\times10^1$: Red(2)-Grey(8)-Brown($\times10^1$), and $\pm10\%$ is Silver.

questions.q: Each resistance in the given cubical network has resistance of 1 $\Omega$ and the equivalent resistance between A and B (the main diagonal of the cube) is
questions.explanation: For a cube of equal resistors R, the resistance between diagonally opposite corners is the standard result $\dfrac{5}{6}R=\dfrac{5}{6}\,\Omega$.

questions.q: A potentiometer has a uniform wire of length 5 m. A battery of emf 10 V and negligible internal resistance is connected between its ends. A secondary cell connected to the circuit gives a balancing length at 200 cm. The emf of the secondary cell is
questions.explanation: Potential gradient $=10/500=0.02$ V/cm; emf $=0.02\times200=4$ V.

questions.q: I-V characteristic of a copper wire of length L and area of cross-section A is shown in figure (a straight line through the origin). The slope of the curve becomes
options: Less if the length of the wire is increased.
More if the experiment is performed at higher temperature.
More if a wire of steel of same dimension is used.
Less if the area of the wire is increased.
questions.explanation: Slope $=I/V=1/R=A/(\rho L)$; increasing the length L increases R and hence decreases the slope, so option (A) is correct (higher temperature or a higher-resistivity steel wire, or larger area, would each change R the opposite way to what B, C, D claim).

questions.q: [Figure shows a resistor network with a 1.2 V battery connected to two identical bridge-like sections in series, each made of 1$\Omega$ resistors, together with a 3$\Omega$ resistor and a 2$\Omega$ resistor in the first section] In the given circuit, the current through 2$\Omega$ resistor is
questions.explanation: Reducing the symmetric network of 1$\Omega$ resistors combined with the 3$\Omega$ and 2$\Omega$ resistors to an equivalent series-parallel circuit and applying Ohm's law across the 1.2 V source gives a current of 0.4 A through the 2$\Omega$ resistor, matching the KEA key.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a reflection of
questions.explanation: The junction rule states that the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it, which is simply a statement of conservation of electric charge.

questions.q: [Figure shows a graph of terminal potential difference V (y-axis, in Volt) versus current I (x-axis, in A) for a cell, a straight line from V = 3 V at I = 0 to V = 0 at I = 6 A] The variation of terminal potential difference (V) with current flowing through a cell is as shown. The emf and internal resistance of the cell are
questions.explanation: The y-intercept gives EMF = 3 V, and internal resistance is the magnitude of the slope: $r = 3/6 = 0.5\Omega$.

questions.q: In a potentiometer experiment, the balancing point with a cell is at a length 240 cm. On shunting the cell with a resistance of 2$\Omega$, the balancing length becomes 120 cm. The internal resistance of the cell is
questions.explanation: Internal resistance $r = R\left(\dfrac{l_1-l_2}{l_2}\right) = 2\times\dfrac{240-120}{120} = 2\Omega$.

questions.q: Though the electron drift velocity is small and electron charge is very small, a conductor can carry an appreciably large current because
options: electron number density is very large
drift velocity of electron is very large
electron number density depends on temperature
questions.explanation: Current $I = neAv_d$; even with small e and $v_d$, the very large free-electron number density n in a conductor makes the current appreciable.

questions.q: Masses of three wires of copper are in the ratio 1:3:5 and their lengths are in the ratio 5:3:1. The ratio of their electrical resistance are
questions.explanation: Since $R = \rho L/A = \rho d L^2/m$ (using $A = m/(dL)$), $R \propto L^2/m$; with masses 1:3:5 and lengths 5:3:1, $R_1:R_2:R_3 = 25/1 : 9/3 : 1/5 = 125:15:1$.

questions.q: Ohm's Law is applicable to
questions.explanation: Ohm's law (V = IR with constant R) holds for metallic conductors at constant temperature, not for non-ohmic devices like diodes, transistors or electrolytes.

questions.q: If the last band on the carbon resistor is absent, then the tolerance is
questions.explanation: By the resistor colour code convention, an absent tolerance band indicates a tolerance of 20%.

questions.q: The effective resistance between P and Q for the following network is [a triangle with R at the top vertex, 3$\Omega$ resistors from R to two mid-nodes, a 6$\Omega$ resistor connecting the two mid-nodes, and 4$\Omega$ and 5$\Omega$ resistors from the mid-nodes down to P and Q respectively]
questions.explanation: Converting the upper delta (3$\Omega$, 3$\Omega$, 6$\Omega$) to a star and combining in series with the 4$\Omega$ and 5$\Omega$ arms gives a net resistance between P and Q of 12 $\Omega$.

questions.q: Five identical resistors each of resistance R = 1500 $\Omega$ are connected to a 300 V battery as shown in the circuit. The reading of the ideal ammeter A is
questions.explanation: Analysing the network of five parallel-branch 1500 $\Omega$ resistors with the ammeter placed as shown, the current recorded by the ideal ammeter works out to 3/5 A.

questions.q: Two cells of internal resistances r$_1$ and r$_2$ and of same emf are connected in series, across a resistor of resistance R. If the terminal potential difference across the cells of internal resistance r$_1$ is zero, then the value of R is
questions.explanation: Terminal p.d. across cell 1 is zero means the current I satisfies I·r$_1$ = emf, i.e. I = emf/r$_1$. Total current I = 2·emf/(r$_1$+r$_2$+R). Equating gives R = r$_1$ − r$_2$.

questions.q: The I–V graphs for two different electrical appliances P and Q are shown in the diagram. If R$_P$ and R$_Q$ be the resistances of the devices, then
questions.explanation: Resistance is the reciprocal of the slope of the I–V graph; since Q has a steeper slope (larger I/V) than P, Q has lower resistance, so R$_P$ > R$_Q$.

questions.q: A cylindrical conductor of diameter 0.1 mm carries a current of 90 mA. The current density (in Am$^{-2}$) is $(\pi \simeq 3)$
A piece of copper is to be shaped into a conducting wire of maximum resistance. The suitable length and diameter are ________ and ________ respectively.
questions.explanation: Since $R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A} \propto \dfrac{L}{d^2}$, resistance is maximised by making the wire as long and as thin as possible — doubling L and halving d gives the largest R among the options.

questions.q: Of the following graphs, the one that correctly represents the I-V. characteristics of a 'Ohmic device' is
options: [graph A: I rises then curves over as V increases]
[graph B: I rises steeply, concave up, as V increases]
[graph C: straight line through the origin]
[graph D: I decreases as V increases]
questions.explanation: An ohmic device obeys $V=IR$ with constant R, giving a straight line I-V graph passing through the origin (graph C).

questions.q: The value of I in the figure shown below is [a square loop with currents 20 A and 4 A entering at the top two corners, 5 A flowing down the left side to the bottom-left corner, 3 A leaving the bottom-left corner, and current I leaving the bottom-right corner]
questions.explanation: By Kirchhoff's current law, total current entering the network equals total current leaving: $20+4 = 3+I \Rightarrow I = 21$ A.

questions.q: The power dissipated in 3Ω resistance in the following circuit is [a 4.5 V cell of internal resistance 1Ω, a 3Ω resistor, a 2Ω resistor and a 6Ω resistor meeting at a common junction, and a 4Ω resistor, all arranged around a circular wire loop]
questions.explanation: Reducing the network (the 2Ω and 6Ω branches combine, in series/parallel with the rest of the loop and the cell's 1Ω internal resistance) to find the current through the 3Ω branch and using $P=I^2R$ gives a dissipated power of 0.75 W, matching the KEA master key.

questions.q: In metre bridge experiment, with a standard resistance in the right gap and a resistance coil dipped in water (in a beaker) in the left gap, the balancing length obtained is 'l'. If the temperature of water is increased, the new balancing length is
questions.explanation: Heating the water raises the coil's (metallic) resistance, so the ratio of left to right resistance increases, which increases the balancing length: new length > l.

questions.q: Mobility of free electrons in a conductor is
questions.explanation: Mobility $\mu = e\tau/m$, so it is directly proportional to the relaxation time $\tau$.

questions.q: Variation of resistance of the conductor with temperature is as shown [Figure: a straight-line graph of R vs T with y-intercept $R_0$ at $T_0$ and slope m]. The temperature co-efficient ($\alpha$) of the conductor is
questions.explanation: $R=R_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]=R_0+(R_0\alpha)(T-T_0)$, so slope $m=R_0\alpha$, giving $\alpha=m/R_0$.

questions.q: Potential difference between A and B in the following circuit [Figure: a single loop with, going from left to right along the top: a 6 V cell, a 2 Ω resistor, point A, a 4 V cell, an 8 Ω resistor, then point B; the loop is completed by a plain wire on the other three sides; the two cells oppose each other around the loop]
questions.explanation: Since the two cells oppose each other around the loop, the net EMF is $6-4=2$ V driving current $I=\dfrac{2}{2+8}=0.2$ A. Going from A to B (with the current) through the 4 V cell (a 4 V drop, since it opposes the current) and the 8 Ω resistor (a further $0.2\times8=1.6$ V drop) gives $V_A-V_B=4+1.6=5.6$ V.

questions.q: In the following network potential at 'O' [Figure: three resistors meet at a common node O — a 2 Ω resistor connects O to point A held at 8 V, a 4 Ω resistor connects O to point B held at 4 V, and a 2 Ω resistor connects O to point C held at 2 V]

Effective resistance between A and B in the following circuit [Figure: a symmetric network of six 10 Ω resistors forming two triangular meshes joined by three connecting resistors, with A and B being the two adjacent nodes on the middle connecting rung]
questions.explanation: Injecting a current at A and extracting it at B and solving the node equations for this network of six 10 Ω resistors shows the two top-corner and left nodes all settle to the same potential by symmetry, and the effective resistance between A and B works out to 10 Ω.

questions.q: Two heating coils of resistances 10 Ω and 20 Ω are connected in parallel and connected to a battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω. The power consumed by them are in the ratio
questions.explanation: The two coils have the same voltage across them (parallel), so $P \propto 1/R$; ratio $P_{10}:P_{20} = 20:10 = 2:1$.

questions.q: The quantity of a charge that will be transferred by a current flow of 20 A over 1 hour 30 minutes period is

Four identical cells of emf E and internal resistance r are to be connected in series. Suppose if one of the cell is connected wrongly, the equivalent emf and effective internal resistance of the combination is
questions.explanation: Reversing one cell subtracts its emf: net emf = 3E − E = 2E; internal resistances still add in series regardless of polarity, giving 4r.

questions.q: Three resistances 2Ω, 3Ω and 4Ω are connected in parallel. The ratio of currents passing through them when a potential difference is applied across its ends will be
questions.explanation: With the same voltage across each, current ∝ 1/R, so the ratio is 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4 = 6 : 4 : 3.

questions.q: Two cells of emf $E_1$ and $E_2$ are joined in opposition (such that $E_1 > E_2$). If $r_1$ and $r_2$ be the internal resistance and R be the external resistance, then the terminal potential difference is [Circuit: cells $E_1$ and $E_2$ with internal resistances $r_1$, $r_2$ connected in opposition, in series with external resistance R.]
questions.explanation: Net emf $=E_1-E_2$ drives current $I=\dfrac{E_1-E_2}{r_1+r_2+R}$; terminal p.d. across R $=IR=\dfrac{(E_1-E_2)R}{r_1+r_2+R}$.

questions.q: In the circuit shown below, the ammeter and the voltmeter readings are 3 A and 6 V respectively. Then the value of the resistance R is [Circuit: an ammeter A in series with resistance R forms one branch; a voltmeter V is connected in parallel across the series combination of A and R.]
questions.explanation: The voltmeter reads the voltage across the ammeter+R branch. Since a real ammeter has a small but non-zero resistance, R = V/I − R_A is slightly less than 6/3 = 2 Ω.

questions.q: In Wheatstone's network P = 2 Ω, Q = 2 Ω, R = 2 Ω and S = 3 Ω. The resistance with which S is to be shunted in order that the bridge may be balanced is
questions.explanation: Balance requires P/Q = R/S', i.e. S' = 2 Ω. Shunting S=3Ω with resistance x to get 2Ω: 1/2 = 1/3 + 1/x, giving x = 6 Ω.

questions.q: The resistance of the bulb filament is 100 Ω at a temperature of 100 °C. If its temperature co-efficient of resistance be 0.005 per °C, its resistance will become 200 Ω at a temperature
A carbon film resistor has colour code Green Black Violet Gold. The value of the resistor is
questions.explanation: Green=5, Black=0, Violet=$10^7$, Gold=$\pm$5%; value = 50\times10^7 $\Omega$ = 500 M$\Omega$ $\pm$5%.

questions.q: Two resistors of resistances 2 $\Omega$ and 6 $\Omega$ are connected in parallel. This combination is then connected to a battery of emf 2V and internal resistance 0.5 $\Omega$. What is the current flowing through the battery?
The equivalent resistance of two resistors connected in series is 6 $\Omega$ and their parallel equivalent resistance is \dfrac{4}{3} $\Omega$. What are the values of resistances?
In a potentiometer experiment of a cell of emf 1.25 V gives balancing length of 30 cm. If the cell is replaced by another cell, balancing length is found to be 40 cm. What is the emf of second cell?
questions.explanation: EMFs are proportional to balancing lengths: E$_2$ = 1.25 \times (40/30) $\approx$ 1.67 V.

questions.q: Three conductors draw currents of 1 A, 2 A and 3 A respectively, when connected in turn across a battery. If they are connected in series and the combination is connected across the same battery, the current drawn will be
questions.explanation: Treating the battery as ideal, each conductor's resistance is $R_i=V/I_i$, so the series current is $I_s=\dfrac{V}{\sum R_i}=\dfrac{1}{\sum(1/I_i)}=\dfrac{1}{1+1/2+1/3}=\dfrac{6}{11}\approx0.545$ A. This does not exactly match any option (closest is 4/7 $\approx$ 0.571 A), so KEA granted grace marks for this question.

questions.q: In the circuit, R$_1$ = R$_2$. The value of E and R$_1$ are ________ (E $-$ EMF, R$_1$ $-$ resistance) [a cell E with internal resistance r = 0 in series with resistor R$_1$; the line then splits into two parallel branches returning to the cell, one containing R$_2$ and the other an unlabelled resistor carrying a current of 1.5 A]
questions.explanation: The second parallel branch's resistance value is not legible/printed on this scanned copy, so the circuit cannot be solved exactly as given; taking that resistor as 10 $\Omega$ reproduces E = 120 V, R$_1$ = 60 $\Omega$ (option 2). KEA granted grace marks for this question, most likely because of a missing value in the original figure.

questions.q: Masses of three wires of copper are in the ratio of 1 : 3 : 5 and their lengths are in the ratio of 5 : 3 : 1. The ratio of their electrical resistances is
questions.explanation: $R=\rho L/A$ and mass $=\rho_d A L$, so $R\propto L^2/\text{mass}$. With $L$ in ratio 5:3:1 and mass in ratio 1:3:5: $R\propto25/1,\,9/3,\,1/5=25:3:0.2=125:15:1$.

questions.q: In the circuit diagram, heat produces in R, 2R and 1.5R are in the ratio of [current enters a parallel combination of resistors R and 2R, which then reconnects in series with a resistor 1.5R before leaving]
questions.explanation: Current splits as $I_R:I_{2R}=2:1$ (inversely as resistance). Heat $\propto I^2R$: $H_R:H_{2R}=\left(\dfrac{2I}{3}\right)^2R:\left(\dfrac{I}{3}\right)^2(2R)=4:2$; with $H_{1.5R}=I^2(1.5R)$, overall $H_R:H_{2R}:H_{1.5R}=\dfrac49:\dfrac29:\dfrac32=8:4:27$.

questions.q: In this circuit, when certain current flows, the heat produced in 5 $\Omega$ is 4.05 J in a time t [figure: 2$\Omega$ in series with a parallel combination of (6$\Omega$+9$\Omega$=15$\Omega$ branch) and a 5$\Omega$ branch]. The heat produced in 2 $\Omega$ coil in the same time interval is
questions.explanation: The 15$\Omega$ and 5$\Omega$ branches (parallel combination 3.75$\Omega$) share the main current I; the 5$\Omega$ branch carries 0.75I, so $(0.75I)^2\times5\times t=4.05$ gives $I^2t=1.44$; heat in 2$\Omega$ = $I^2\times2\times t$ = 2.88 J.

questions.q: In this circuit, the value of I$_2$ is [figure: a current of 1.2 A splits into three parallel branches: I$_1$ through 10$\Omega$, I$_2$ through 15$\Omega$, I$_3$ through 30$\Omega$]
questions.explanation: Current divides in inverse proportion to resistance; I$_2$ = 1.2 $\times$ (1/15)/(1/10+1/15+1/30) = 1.2$\times$(1/15)/(1/5) = 0.4 A.

questions.q: Which of the following graphs correctly represents the variation of heat energy (U) produced in a metallic conductor in a given time as a function of potential difference (V) across the conductor? [four U vs V graphs]
options: a straight line through the origin
a curve that rises then flattens (concave down)
a curve that falls from a high value toward zero
a curve that rises increasingly steeply (concave up, like a parabola through the origin)
questions.explanation: For an ohmic conductor $U=V^2t/R$, a parabola through the origin that rises increasingly steeply with V, matching graph (4).

questions.q: A current of 2 A is passing through a metal wire of cross sectional area 2$\times$10$^{-6}$ m$^2$. If the number density of free electrons in the wire is 5$\times$10$^{26}$ m$^{-3}$, the drift speed of electrons is (given e = 1.6$\times$10$^{-19}$ C)

In the circuit shown, the currents $i_1$ and $i_2$ are ............... [Circuit: a $12\,\Omega$ resistor (carrying current $i_1$) is in parallel with a $4\,\Omega$ resistor (carrying current $i_2$); this parallel combination is in series with a $2\,\Omega$ resistor, connected to a battery of 12 V with internal resistance $1\,\Omega$]
questions.explanation: Parallel combination of $12\,\Omega$ and $4\,\Omega$ is $3\,\Omega$; total circuit resistance $=3+2+1=6\,\Omega$, total current $=12/6=2$ A, which splits inversely to resistance: $i_1$ (through $12\,\Omega$) $=2\times4/16=0.5$ A, $i_2$ (through $4\,\Omega$) $=2\times12/16=1.5$ A.

questions.q: A conductor wire having $10^{29}$ free electrons/$m^3$ carries a current of 20A. If the cross-section of the wire is 1 $mm^2$, then the drift velocity of electrons will be ............... ($e = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C).
A resistor has a colour code of green, blue, brown and silver. What is its resistance?
questions.explanation: Green=5, Blue=6, Brown=multiplier $10^1$, Silver=$\pm10\%$ tolerance, giving $56\times10=560\,\Omega\pm10\%$.

questions.q: The voltage $V$ and current $I$ graphs for a conductor at two different temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ are shown in the figure. The relation between $T_1$ and $T_2$ is ............. [Graph of V versus I: line $T_1$ is steeper (closer to the V-axis) than line $T_2$]
questions.explanation: The slope of the V-I graph gives resistance; the steeper line ($T_1$) has higher resistance, and since resistance of a conductor increases with temperature, $T_1>T_2$.

questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding the network shown in the figure. [Network: from A to B there are two parallel arms; the top arm has two resistors $R$ and $R$ in series with a galvanometer $G$ connected between their junction and the junction of the bottom arm; the bottom arm has two resistors $2R$ and $2R$ in series; a battery $E$ is connected between A and B] a) The equivalent resistance of the network between points A and B is independent of value of G. b) The equivalent resistance of the network between points A and B is $\dfrac{4}{3}R$. c) The current through G is zero. Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.explanation: The bridge is balanced since $R/R=2R/2R$, so no current flows through $G$ (c true) and the resistance is independent of $G$ (a true); the equivalent resistance is then the parallel combination of the two arms $2R$ (top) and $4R$ (bottom): $\dfrac{2R\times4R}{2R+4R}=\dfrac{4}{3}R$ (b true), so all three statements are true.

questions.q: A battery of e.m.f. $E$ has an internal resistance 'r'. A variable resistance $R$ is connected to the terminals of the battery. A current $I$ is drawn from the battery. $V$ is the terminal P.D. If $R$ alone is gradually reduced to zero, which of the following best describes $I$ and $V$?
questions.explanation: $I=E/(R+r)\to E/r$ as $R\to0$ (finite, since $r\neq0$); $V=E-Ir\to E-(E/r)r=0$.

questions.q: Three voltmeters $A$, $B$ and $C$ having resistances $R$, $1.5R$ and $3R$ respectively are used in a circuit as shown [$X$ connects through $A$ to a node, from which $B$ and $C$ are in parallel, joining at $Y$]. When a P.D. is applied between $X$ and $Y$, the reading of the voltmeters are $V_1$, $V_2$ and $V_3$ respectively. Then .....................
questions.explanation: $B$ and $C$ in parallel give $R_{BC}=\dfrac{1.5R\times3R}{4.5R}=R$, equal to $R_A$. The same current flows through $A$ and through the $B$–$C$ combination, and since their resistances are equal, $V_1=V_2=V_3$.

questions.q: In the circuit given here, the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are 70 V, zero, 10 V respectively [a $10\,\Omega$ resistor joins $A$ to node $D$, a $20\,\Omega$ resistor joins $D$ to $B$, and a $30\,\Omega$ resistor joins $D$ to $C$]. Then
options: currents in the paths $AD$, $DB$ and $DC$ are in the ratio of 1 : 2 : 3
currents in the paths $AD$, $DB$ and $DC$ are in the ratio of 3 : 2 : 1
the point $D$ will be at a potential of 60 V
the point $D$ will be at a potential of 20 V
questions.explanation: Applying KCL at $D$: $(70-V_D)/10=V_D/20+(V_D-10)/30\Rightarrow V_D=40$ V. Currents: $I_{AD}=3$ A, $I_{DB}=2$ A, $I_{DC}=1$ A, ratio $3:2:1$. (KEA awarded grace marks for this question, possibly due to the option printed as 'AB' instead of 'AD'.)

questions.q: $B_1$, $B_2$ and $B_3$ are the three identical bulbs connected to a battery of steady e.m.f. with key $K$ closed [$B_1$ in series with $K$; $B_2$ and $B_3$ in parallel with each other, this combination in series with $B_1$]. What happens to the brightness of the bulbs $B_1$ and $B_2$ when the key is opened?
options: Brightness of the bulb, $B_1$ decreases and that of $B_2$ increases.
Brightness of the bulbs $B_1$ and $B_2$ decreases.
Brightness of the bulbs $B_1$ increases and that of $B_2$ decreases.
Brightness of the bulbs $B_1$ and $B_2$ increases.
questions.explanation: With $K$ closed, $B_1$ carries the full circuit current while $B_2$ and $B_3$ share it equally. Opening $K$ (which controls the $B_3$ branch) increases the total resistance, so the current through $B_1$ decreases (dimmer); this reduced current now flows entirely through $B_2$, which is more than $B_2$'s earlier share, so $B_2$ brightens.

The resistance of a wire at 300 K is found to be $0.3\ \Omega$. If the temperature co-efficient of resistance of wire is $1.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, the temperature at which the resistance becomes $0.6\ \Omega$ is
questions.explanation: Using $R_T=R_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]$: $2=1+1.5\times10^{-3}\Delta T \Rightarrow \Delta T \approx 667\ \text{K}$, giving $T\approx967\ \text{K}$ (closest option, 993 K, as per KEA key).

questions.q: Three resistors $1\ \Omega$, $2\ \Omega$, and $3\ \Omega$ are connected to form a triangle. Across $3\ \Omega$ resistor a 3 V battery is connected. The current through $3\ \Omega$ resistor is
questions.explanation: The battery's two terminals are the same two nodes across the $3\ \Omega$ resistor, so full 3 V appears directly across it: $I=V/R=3/3=1$ A (the $1\Omega+2\Omega$ series path is a separate parallel branch).

questions.q: The accurate measurement of emf can be obtained using
questions.explanation: A potentiometer at balance draws no current from the cell, so it measures the true emf accurately, unlike a voltmeter which draws some current.
